intro: Japan's first capital kept its trees the way it kept its temples, as part of the religion. Nara Park is not a park in the European sense but the shared grounds of Kasuga Taisha and Todai-ji, where deer have grazed for centuries and cutting a tree needed a reason. The result is a city whose oldest living things stand in the open with rope tied around them: a camphor that has watched a thousand years of festivals, a cedar drawn as a sapling in 1309, and a hollow trunk with a bamboo growing out of the top.
meta_description: Nara's oldest tree is a camphor of a thousand years, twelve metres round at the base. That, a cedar drawn as a sapling in 1309, and thirteen more.
question_meta: Nara's oldest tree is the thousand-year camphor of Naratsuhiko Shrine, twelve metres round at the base and a protected natural monument since 1951.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Nara is the giant camphor behind the main hall of Naratsuhiko Shrine on the old Narazaka pass road, recorded as over a thousand years old and protected as a Nara Prefecture Natural Monument since 1951. It measures 12.8 metres around at ground level and roughly thirty metres tall, forking into two great limbs about seven metres up. It is free to visit.
question_context: The age is traditional rather than measured, as it is for almost every great camphor in Japan, but the size supports it and the shrine's own founding legend puts it at twelve centuries. What makes this tree worth the fifteen minute bus ride is what happens beneath it. On the evening of the eighth of October each year the shrine performs the Okina-mai, a masked dance recognised as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property and one of the oldest surviving ancestors of Noh theatre, and it is danced in the camphor's shade. The tree stands on Narazaka, the pass that carried travellers into the capital from the north, so anyone arriving in Nara from Kyoto in the eighth century walked past it. The only serious rival for the title is the great cedar at Kasuga Taisha, which sources date at somewhere between eight hundred and a thousand years and which has the better documentary evidence.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Nara?
faq.a: The giant camphor of Naratsuhiko Shrine, over a thousand years old and 12.8 metres around at the base. A prefectural natural monument since 1951, and free to visit.

faq.q: Which Nara tree has the best story?
faq.a: The great cedar at Kasuga Taisha. It appears as a young sapling in a picture scroll donated to the shrine in 1309, and a second tree growing from its base was allowed through a hole cut in the roof of the hall beside it rather than be cut down.

faq.q: When should I visit for blossom?
faq.a: Late March. The weeping cherry at Himuro Shrine is known as Nara's first cherry because it opens before any other in the city, and the five-colour camellia at Byakugo-ji flowers from late March into mid-April.

faq.q: Are these trees free to see?
faq.a: Most are. Everything in Nara Park is open ground, and Naratsuhiko and Himuro shrines cost nothing. Byakugo-ji charges 500 yen and involves over a hundred stone steps.

trees.name: The Giant Camphor of Naratsuhiko Shrine
trees.story: Twelve point eight metres around at the ground, and it holds a rope. This camphor stands behind the main hall of a shrine on Narazaka, the pass road that carried travellers into Japan's first permanent capital from the north, which means anyone walking into Nara from Kyoto in the eighth century passed beneath it. It rises about thirty metres and forks into two great limbs some seven metres up, each of which forks again, so from below the crown reads less like a tree than like several trees agreeing to share a base. The prefecture designated it a natural monument in 1951. What makes it worth the bus ride rather than merely worth reading about is the eighth of October. On that evening the shrine performs the Okina-mai, a masked dance recognised as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property and one of the oldest surviving ancestors of Noh theatre, and it is danced here, under this tree, as it has been for centuries. Be honest about the thousand years: like almost every great camphor in Japan, the figure is traditional rather than measured. The girth supports it.
trees.transport: Bus from JR or Kintetsu Nara toward Aoyama Jutaku, about 15 min, alight at Narazaka
trees.notes: Age is traditional, not dated: no source gives a method. The 1951 prefectural designation, the measurements and the Okina-mai connection are all independently sourced. Coordinates are the individually mapped tree, not the shrine centroid.
trees.verify_notes: Girth and height from the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース), the only record for クスノキ at 奈良豆比古神社. Survey figures, so the tree has grown since. The two girth figures are both right and measure different things: 12.8 m is at the ground, as the story says, and the 800 cm in girth_cm is the Environment Ministry's survey at 130 cm, which is the standard the rankings compare on.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk forking into two great limbs about seven metres up, each forking again, with a rope tied around it. It stands behind the main hall at Naratsuhiko Shrine.

trees.name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha
trees.story: There is a picture scroll, donated to this shrine in 1309, in which this cedar appears as a sapling. Seven centuries later it is roughly eight metres around and twenty-five tall, standing beside the hall where offerings are shared after the rituals, and the sapling in the painting is the same organism. Almost no ancient tree anywhere can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. The better story is what grows out of its base. A second tree, a shinpaku, took root there and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof and let it through. The hall still has the hole. Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768 for the deity of the Fujiwara clan and rebuilt every twenty years for centuries, so the buildings around this cedar are younger than the cedar, repeatedly. One practical note before you go: sources place the tree beside the Naoraiden near the inner gate, and it is not clear from the shrine's own pages whether that spot falls inside the free outer precinct or the paid inner one.
trees.access: Kasuga Taisha precinct, open 06:00 to 18:00; the outer grounds are free, and it is unclear whether this tree stands inside the paid inner area, so check on arrival
trees.transport: About 25 to 30 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden
trees.notes: Sources disagree on age (800 to 1,000 per the national multilingual database, about 1,000 in the mapped record) and on girth (7.94m against 8.7m, likely different measuring heights); both ranges are reported rather than resolved. The access zone genuinely could not be confirmed and is stated as uncertain.
trees.verify_notes: Girth and height from the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース), the only record for スギ (春日大社の大杉) at 春日大社, surveyed 2000年6月21日. Survey figures, so the tree has grown since.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the second tree growing from its base, reaching toward the neighbouring hall through a hole cut in the roof. It stands beside the Naoraiden, near Kasuga Taisha's inner gate.

trees.name: The Five-Colour Camellia of Byakugo-ji
trees.story: One tree, five colours, and it does not drop its flowers the way a camellia is supposed to. This four hundred year old camellia opens red, white and peach blossoms on the same plant, along with striped and variegated ones, which is how it earned its name and its place among the three famous camellias of Nara. Most camellias shed the whole flower head at once, which is why the Japanese associated them with beheading and why samurai were said to dislike them; this one is a chiri-tsubaki, shedding petal by petal instead, so the ground beneath it in April is a scatter of loose colour rather than a row of fallen heads. It is only about five metres tall. The prefecture designated it a natural monument in 1957. Byakugo-ji itself sits on a hillside at the southeastern edge of the city with the whole Nara basin spread out below, which is the compensation for the climb: over a hundred stone steps stand between the bus stop and the tree, and there is no way around them.
trees.access: Paid, 500 yen for adults, open 09:00 to 17:00; over 100 stone steps from the road, not step-free
trees.transport: Bus from Nara station toward Takabatake, then about 10 min walk and the steps
trees.notes: Age given as about 400 by most sources and 450 by one; the range covers both. No openly licensed photograph of this tree exists on Wikimedia Commons or iNaturalist, searched by Japanese name, by romanised name and by geosearch of the temple. A genuine gap.

best_time.label: late March into mid-April, when one tree opens red, white and pink at once

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its blossoms, red, white, peach, striped and variegated all on the same plant, shedding petal by petal rather than whole. It stands atop over a hundred stone steps at Byakugo-ji.

trees.name: The Soapberry with a Bamboo Through It

location.address: Nara Park, beside the approach to Kasuga Taisha near the Nara National Museum

trees.story: The trunk is hollow, and a bamboo has grown up inside it and out through the top. Bamboo from the tea house grove behind found the cavity in this soapberry, went up through it and emerged from the crown, so what stands on the bend of the Kasuga approach is one tree wearing another. The shrine's own guide describes the effect as a mother holding a child. At four and a half metres around and over fifteen tall it is claimed as the largest soapberry in Nara Prefecture, and nobody has published an age for it, which is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a number. Its black seeds had two jobs. Strung, they became prayer beads. Loose, they were the weights inside the shuttlecocks of hanetsuki, the New Year battledore game, which is why the tree turns up in old accounts of the season. The pulp around them lathers in water, and that is where the English name comes from: this is the tree people washed with before soap was cheap.
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, beside the Nara National Museum
trees.notes: No published age exists; the range is inferred from girth alone and is the weakest figure on this page. Girth is 4.58m per the mapped record and 470cm per the giant-tree society, consistent. No openly licensed photograph found.

best_time.label: October and November, when the translucent amber fruit ripens

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bamboo growing up through its hollow trunk and out through the crown. It stands on the bend of the Kasuga Taisha approach, near the Nara National Museum.

trees.name: The Camphors of Tobihino
trees.story: Three trees planted in 1908 have grown into one cloud. They stand in a ring fence in the middle of the Tobihino meadow, marking the spot where Emperor Meiji sat to watch army manoeuvres, and in a little over a century they have closed into a single dome so complete that most people photograph them believing they are looking at one enormous tree. The largest trunk is nearly five metres around and the crown reaches twenty-six metres. What makes the spot rather than the tree is everything else in the frame: open grass, morning mist off the hills behind, and the deer of Nara Park grazing right up to the fence, because Tobihino is where they gather. This is the youngest tree on this page by several centuries and it earns its place on presence alone. Come early. The meadow faces east, the light comes in under the crown, and the deer are out before the buses are.
trees.access: Free, open meadow at all hours
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from Kintetsu Nara
trees.notes: Two different camphors stand on this meadow and local sources use overlapping names: the Environment Ministry places the three Meiji memorial trees (4.8m, 26m, about 140 years) here, while another source places a separate hollow camphor of 7.07m girth at the south end. The confirmed coordinate and the measurements match the Meiji triplets, which is what this entry describes. Photo licence and framing recorded but not yet viewed at full size, so it stays unapproved.
trees.verify_notes: Girth 480 cm and height 26 m from the Environment Ministry's own Nara Park giant-tree course guide, which names this entry クスノキ三兄弟, the three camphor brothers, on the north side of Tobihino, and dates them to a commemorative planting at the spot where the Meiji emperor sat during the 1908 army manoeuvres. NOT applied: a separate ministry database record at 春日野町飛火野 reads 1110 cm with an age band of 99年以下. It is not attached here because this entry is an ensemble and hanging a single-trunk figure on an ensemble is a bridge claim; which trunk carries 1110 cm is an open question for a verify pass.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its three trunks grown into one dome-shaped crown, inside a ring fence with deer grazing up to it. It stands in the middle of the Tobihino meadow, in Nara Park.

trees.name: The Great Nagi of Kasuga Taisha

location.address: Kasuga Taisha precinct, north of the Treasure Hall, 160 Kasugano-cho, Nara

trees.story: This tree should not be here at all. Nagi grows wild in Kyushu and Taiwan, far to the south, and the nine hectares of it on this hillside are the northernmost stand of its kind, a national natural monument since 1923. Nara City's own record is blunt about why: the grove is not natural. Trees were offered to the shrine during the Nara period and the descendants of those offerings spread across the slope, so what looks like ancient woodland is the result of twelve centuries of donation. This individual is the largest of them, three and a third metres around and thirteen metres tall, which for a species this slow is why estimates run to five centuries and beyond. It is a conifer that has forgotten how to look like one: the leaves are broad, leathery ovals with parallel veins running end to end and no midrib at all, so people who know their trees stop, look again, and go and read the sign. The city protected the tree itself in 1997, along with a twenty metre square of ground around it.
trees.access: Kasuga Taisha precinct; outer grounds free, check on arrival which zone this tree falls in
trees.transport: About 25 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden
trees.notes: The city's cultural-properties page dates the grove to roughly 1,000 years while the Environment Ministry gives this individual 500 or more; both are reported. Position is sourced as 'north of the Treasure Hall' with no published coordinate, so the pin is the Treasure Hall area and precision is approximate.
trees.verify_notes: CORRECTED 2026-09-08 within the hour: a first pass took 342 cm and 18 m from the giant-tree database on the reasoning that it was the only ナギ recorded at 春日大社. Kasuga Taisha holds an entire nagi grove, 春日大社ナギ樹林, which is itself a natural monument, so 'the only one in the database' is not 'the only one there'. The ministry's own Nara Park course guide gives 330 cm and 13 m for the tree north of the treasure hall at over 500 years, which is this entry and agrees with our age. Those are the figures used.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, broad leathery ovals with parallel veins and no midrib at all, on what is actually a conifer. It is the largest of the grove, north of the Treasure Hall.

trees.name: The First Cherry of Nara
trees.story: Nara's spring officially starts at this tree. The weeping cherry standing beside the approach to Himuro Shrine opens before any other cherry in the city, which earned it the name Nara ichiban zakura, first cherry of Nara, and turns a quiet shrine into a queue for about ten days in late March. It leans over the pond in front of the gate, so the flowers arrive twice, once above you and once in the water. The shrine underneath it is stranger than the tree. It stands on the site of a Nara period ice house and enshrines the deity of ice: blocks were cut in winter, packed into a pit insulated with straw and kept through the summer for the imperial court, and ice merchants still come here to pray for their trade. Every year at the end of May the shrine holds a festival where offerings are made in ice, including whole fish frozen inside blocks. The tree is young by the standards of this page, and its hundred years rests on a single source, so treat the number lightly and the timing seriously.
trees.transport: Bus to Himuro Jinja / Kokuritsu Hakubutsukan, which stops at the gate, or about 15 min walk from Nara station
trees.notes: The age figure comes from a single source and is treated as soft. The bloom timing is well sourced. Photo licence recorded but not yet viewed at full size, so it stays unapproved rather than trusted.

best_time.label: late March, when it opens before every other cherry in Nara

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the way it leans out over the pond in front of the shrine gate. It stands beside the approach to Himuro Shrine.

trees.name: The Chinaberry of the East Pagoda Ruins

location.address: Nara Park, about 100 m east of the Todai-ji East Pagoda ruins

trees.story: It stands on ground that once held one of the tallest buildings in Japan. Todai-ji's east pagoda rose seven storeys and is reported at around a hundred metres, burned, was rebuilt, burned again and was never rebuilt a third time, so all that remains is a raised platform in the grass with a chinaberry beside it four and a half metres around and twenty metres tall. Nobody has published its age. What is recorded is the reason its species turns up in places like this: chinaberry was believed to drive off evil spirits and was traditionally planted in graveyards and at sites where the dead were remembered, which is exactly what a burned pagoda platform became. For most of the year it is an unremarkable spreading tree that visitors walk past on their way to the Great Buddha. For two weeks in the middle of May it covers itself in loose sprays of pale purple flowers, and the official guide to Nara Park's giant trees singles that fortnight out as the reason to come.
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 20 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, in the grounds between Todai-ji and the park
trees.notes: Age is explicitly not recorded by the Environment Ministry's own guide, which is the single substantive source for the tree itself; the range is inferred from girth. Position is sourced as about 100m east of the pagoda ruins, so the pin is approximate. The flowering month comes from that same official guide.

best_time.label: mid-May, when it covers itself in pale purple sprays

trees.verify_notes: Girth 450 cm and height 20 m from the ministry's Nara Park course guide, which places the tree 100 m east of the East Pagoda ruins, and that is where our pin already stood. The giant-tree database's 2000 survey of the same tree reads 425 cm and 15 m, so it has put on roughly 25 cm of girth since.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, right beside the raised platform of the burnt east pagoda, four and a half metres round. For a fortnight in mid-May it carries loose sprays of pale purple flowers.

trees.name: The Thickest Black Pine of Nara Park

location.address: Nara Park, northeast corner of the Kofuku-ji National Treasure Hall block

trees.story: Black pines were planted through Nara Park for centuries for no reason except that they looked right, and this is the fattest survivor of that long habit: three and a half metres around, twenty-eight metres tall, and roughly two hundred and fifty years old, which puts its planting in the middle of the Edo period. It is also the easiest tree on this page to reach, about five minutes from the station, standing at the corner of the block that holds Kofuku-ji's National Treasure Hall. Look at the ground under it before you look up. Flying squirrels live in the park and strip the cones for their seeds, leaving the gnawed cores scattered beneath the tree in a shape the locals compare to fried prawns, so a handful of little stripped spindles on the path is the sign that something was in the crown overnight. The official guide to the park's giant trees ends its entry on this tree by remarking that the Edo period gardeners who put it here would be pleased with how it turned out, which is a fair summary of the whole park.
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 5 min walk from Kintetsu Nara
trees.notes: The Environment Ministry's park guide is the single substantive source for this individual, giving girth, height and an estimated 250 years. Position is sourced by description rather than coordinate, so the pin is approximate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the thickest pine in the park, 3.54 metres round, at the corner of the Kofuku-ji National Treasure Hall block. Look for the gnawed cone cores the flying squirrels leave underneath.

trees.name: The Roben-sugi of Nigatsu-do
trees.age_estimate: current tree roughly 60 years old, replanted after 1961
trees.story:
An eagle carried off a baby and left it in a cedar on this slope, and the baby grew up to found Todai-ji. That is the legend of the Roben-sugi. The infant was Roben, later the temple's first abbot, found and raised by a monk, and the tree on the spot has carried his name ever since. A stone monument beside it records the story.

This is not that cedar, and nobody here pretends it is. The original lived roughly six hundred years and reached 21.2 metres before the Second Muroto Typhoon came through Nara on 16 September 1961 with winds recorded at 75 metres a second. What happened afterwards is where the accounts part. One says the replacement failed to take and the tree standing today went in on 16 March 1967, raised from the one that died. Another calls this the fourth generation rather than the third. They disagree about how many attempts it took, not about whether this one has held.

So it is roughly sixty years old, which makes it the youngest tree on this page. Nara is a good place to be relaxed about that. The address is the relic here, not the timber.

It stands below the slope Nigatsu-do occupies, immediately north of the small Kojo Shrine, on the surveyed spot OpenStreetMap records for it. Free, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct, and the climb up is short.
trees.access: Free, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct (Nigatsu-do itself has no admission fee)
trees.transport: City loop bus from Kintetsu Nara Station to Daibutsuden Kasuga Taisha-mae, then about 15 min walk uphill
trees.notes: Sources agree the original Roben-sugi was destroyed by the Second Muroto Typhoon on 16 September 1961 and that today's tree is a replanting; they disagree on whether it is the third or the fourth generation, which is stated in the story rather than resolved. Pin is shrine-level: sources place the tree below Nigatsu-do's slope immediately north of Kojo Shrine, and the coordinate is mapped from that description, not from a register or a survey.
trees.how_to_recognise: A young, narrow cedar standing on its own in the open court below Nigatsu-do, branches down to the ground and a stone monument at its foot. The thick old cedars further along the slope are not it.

trees.name: The Kaya of Nigatsu-do
trees.age_estimate: 200 to 299 years, from the national survey's age band

location.address: Nigatsu-do, Todai-ji outer precinct, Zoshi-cho, Nara

trees.story:
Nara's most famous tree at Nigatsu-do is a cedar of about sixty years, a replanting after the typhoon of 1961. Four metres round and two to three centuries old, this one is neither famous nor young, and almost nobody looks at it.

It is a kaya, Torreya nucifera, which is not a common thing to find at this size anywhere. The species grows so slowly that its timber is the material Japanese go and shogi boards are cut from, and a single board can take a tree's lifetime to earn. Four hundred and ten centimetres of girth on a kaya is therefore a great deal more time than the same figure on a cedar or a camphor. The national survey put it at twenty-seven metres and in good health, and recorded that it can be picked out from a distance, which on this slope means from the path below rather than from among the buildings.

Nigatsu-do is the hall whose balcony gives the view back over Nara, and where the Omizutori fire and water rites run every March. The tree stands in that company without a plaque or a legend to its name.
trees.access: Free, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct, open in daylight
trees.transport: About 20 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, uphill past Sangatsu-do
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad, dark, blunt-needled conifer, not a cedar: kaya needles are flat, stiff and sharp at the tip, and the crown spreads rather than tapers. It is the only Torreya the national survey records at Nigatsu-do.
trees.notes: Single-sourced on the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース, PDL 1.0, report 47076), which measured it in the 1988 to 2000 national survey and gives no coordinate. The pin is Nigatsu-do itself, not the trunk. Species is unique to this facility in that survey, which is what makes the identification safe; the exact stand needs a visit.

trees.name: The Saw-leaf Zelkova of Tamukeyama Hachimangu
trees.age_estimate: 200 to 299 years, from the national survey's age band
trees.story:
Twenty-eight metres of zelkova on a shrine slope that most visitors cross without stopping, on their way between the Great Buddha and Nigatsu-do.

Keyaki is the tree Japanese carpentry is built out of. Temple pillars, drum shells, the great beams of a hall: when a Japanese building needed timber that would hold a load for three hundred years, this was the species it was cut from. The irony of a four-metre keyaki standing in a temple precinct is that a tree this good was usually felled long before it got here. This one was measured at four hundred and five centimetres round in the national giant-tree survey, in good health, and it is the only zelkova the survey records at this shrine.

Tamukeyama Hachimangu sits on the rise immediately south of Nigatsu-do, and is the shrine that was brought to Nara in the eighth century to watch over the casting of the Great Buddha. In autumn the slope turns, and a zelkova is one of the reasons: the species goes copper rather than yellow.
trees.transport: About 20 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, on the path between Todai-ji and Nigatsu-do
trees.how_to_recognise: The vase shape gives it away: a keyaki splits into a fan of near-equal limbs low down and spreads outward, unlike the single leading trunk of the cedars around it. The only zelkova the national survey records at this shrine.
trees.notes: Single-sourced on the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース, PDL 1.0, report 47079). No coordinate exists in that source; the pin is the shrine, not the trunk. The autumn colour is a species trait rather than a recorded observation of this tree.

trees.name: The Great Camphor of Wakamiya
trees.age_estimate: over 300 years, from the national survey's age band

location.address: Kasuga Taisha Wakamiya Shrine, Kasugano-cho, Nara

trees.story:
Five hundred and seventy-eight centimetres round and thirty metres tall, which makes this the largest tree on the Kasuga side of Nara Park that is not inside the paid precinct.

Camphor is the giant of warm Japan, and this is what the species does when nobody cuts it: a heavy, low, wide trunk carrying a crown the size of a small building, evergreen, and aromatic enough that a broken leaf smells of the stuff medicine cabinets used to smell of. The national survey put it at over three hundred years and recorded part of the crown as dying back, which is normal in a camphor of this age and not a sign of a tree in trouble.

How big it is exactly is an open question, and this page would rather say so than pick a number. The ministry measured five hundred and seventy-eight centimetres at chest height. OpenStreetMap, which also carries the tree and marks it as a natural monument, records twelve and a half metres round. Both cannot be measuring the same thing.

It stands at Wakamiya, the shrine at the end of the stone lantern avenue south of Kasuga Taisha's main hall, where the On-matsuri procession has come every December without a break since 1136.
trees.access: Free, open shrine grounds; the Kasuga Taisha inner precinct charges but Wakamiya does not
trees.transport: About 30 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden and 10 min on foot
trees.how_to_recognise: The only camphor of this size at Wakamiya: a single massive low trunk with a wide evergreen crown, unmistakable among the cedars and the stone lanterns. OpenStreetMap marks it as a natural monument at this exact point.
trees.notes: Girth, height, age band and vitality from the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース, PDL 1.0, report 47078), which gives no coordinate. The pin is an OpenStreetMap node 41 m from the shrine point, tagged Cinnamomum camphora and denotation=natural_monument, which corroborates species, existence and position independently. UNRESOLVED: that node also carries circumference=12.46 and height=24 against the ministry's 578 cm and 30 m. The likeliest reconciliation is that the two measured at different heights, since the ministry measures girth at 130 cm and records this as a single stem rather than a multi-stem, but nobody here has seen the trunk. The page says so rather than picking a number quietly.

trees.name: The Enoki of Wakamiya
trees.age_estimate: 200 to 299 years, from the national survey's age band

location.address: Kasuga Taisha Wakamiya Shrine, Kasugano-cho, Nara

trees.story:
Five metres round and only seventeen metres tall, which is the shape a hackberry takes when it has had room and time: squat, heavy in the trunk, and spread out sideways rather than up.

Enoki is a tree Japan planted deliberately at the roadside, on the earth mounds that marked each ri along the old highways, because it grows fast, casts a wide shade and is easy to see from a distance. Todai-ji has one of those milestone trees at its West Gate site. This one is not that: it stands on shrine ground at Wakamiya, and nothing recorded says why it is here. What the national survey does say is that it is over five hundred centimetres in girth, two to three centuries old, and in good health, which for a species most people walk past without naming is a considerable tree.

It shares the ground with the great camphor a few steps away, so the two are one stop rather than two, at the quiet end of the stone lantern avenue below Kasuga Taisha.
trees.transport: About 30 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden and 10 min on foot
trees.how_to_recognise: Squat and wide rather than tall, with a heavy short trunk and small toothed leaves, standing near the great camphor. The only hackberry the national survey records at Wakamiya.
trees.notes: Single-sourced on the Environment Ministry's giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース, PDL 1.0, report 47073). No coordinate in the source; the pin is the shrine, not the trunk. The milestone-planting habit is a general fact about the species and about Todai-ji's West Gate tree, explicitly not a claim about this one.

trees.name: The Great Ginkgo of Haraedo Shrine
trees.age_estimate: over 300 years, from the national survey's age band

location.address: Haraedo Shrine, Kasuga Taisha, Kasugano-cho, Nara
location.neighbourhood: Kasuga Taisha, on the approach between the Second Torii and Nanmon Gate

trees.story:
Before you reach Kasuga Taisha itself, the approach path stops at a small purification shrine, Haraedo, where visitors were traditionally meant to be cleansed before going on to the main sanctuary. Its ginkgo has stood over that ritual for more than three centuries.

Four metres and thirty centimetres round and twenty-five metres tall, with some dieback in the crown by the time the national survey measured it in 2000, which for a tree this size is ordinary rather than a warning. Ginkgo biloba is the oldest surviving tree lineage on Earth, essentially unchanged for two hundred million years, and it exists today mostly because people kept planting it around temples and shrines for a thousand years rather than because it thrives in the wild. This one earned its place at Haraedo the way most did, as a shrine tree rather than a survivor of anything.

Kasuga Taisha's own walking guide names it directly, the only ginkgo it names anywhere on either of its two forest routes, and says plainly what to come back for: not the ritual, but late autumn, when the tree turns and draws people who never knew Haraedo existed.

It stands on the free public approach, well before the ticketed inner precinct that holds the shrine's famous stone lanterns, so nobody needs a ticket to see it turn.
trees.access: Free, on the open public approach path to Kasuga Taisha, before the paid inner precinct
trees.transport: About 30 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden and a few minutes on foot
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the only ginkgo Kasuga Taisha's own walking guide names, standing at Haraedo Shrine on the approach between the Second Torii and Nanmon Gate, well before the ticketed precinct.

best_time.label: November, when the ginkgo turns gold

trees.notes: Register: Environment Ministry giant-tree database (巨樹・巨木林データベース, PDL 1.0), report 47074, facility 春日大社, girth 430cm, height 25m, age band 300+ years, surveyed 2000-06-21 (so likely over 320 years by now), health shows some dieback (alive_hint true), no official designation. Second source: Kasuga Taisha's own official site (kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/morisanpo2/, fetched via a Wayback Machine snapshot since the live page hangs on direct fetch) names and photographs 祓戸神社の大イチョウ (Great Ginkgo of Haraedo Shrine) as a specific stop on its own course between the Second Torii and Nanmon Gate, the only ginkgo named on either of its two forest-walk pages, which is what makes it safe to treat as the same tree as the register row rather than a different giant ginkgo elsewhere on the grounds. No independent girth figure was found to cross-check the register's 430cm. No coordinate in either source; the pin is the Kasuga Taisha facility point, not the trunk.
